title: The Old Babylonian 'Yale tablet'
short: This part of Thompson's Tablet III comes from the Old Babylonian Yale tablet, which tells of the plans for the expedition to the Cedar Forest.
body: Thompson notes that the text 'down to this point' is the Assyrian version restored from the Old Babylonian; this opening speech is notoriously obscure, and Thompson thinks it may be a farewell formula. The Yale tablet, published by Jastrow and Clay (1920), contains the friends' discussion of Huwawa, the elders' warnings and the forging of weapons. In George's edition these episodes belong to the Old Babylonian Tablet III and the standard Tablets II-III; much of the standard text was still unknown in 1928.

title: The Forest of Cedars
short: The Cedar Forest, home of the gods and guarded by Humbaba, lies in the far mountains: in the standard version, in Lebanon.
body: Cedar wood was the most precious timber in treeless Mesopotamia, used for temple doors and roof-beams, and kings boasted of expeditions to fetch it. In the Sumerian poem 'Gilgamesh and Huwawa' the forest lies in the east; the Akkadian versions point to the west, to Lebanon and the Anti-Lebanon (Jastrow and Clay already placed it there). George discusses the shift. The forest is also sacred, a 'dwelling of the gods', so the expedition is ambiguous: heroic quest for fame, but also an assault on divine property. The Sulaymaniyah tablet of Tablet V (2014) depicts it as a noisy jungle full of monkeys, cicadas and birds.

title: Humbaba (Huwawa), guardian of the Forest
short: Humbaba is the monstrous guardian of the Cedar Forest, appointed by Enlil to terrify mortals.
body: The Old Babylonian form is Huwawa; Jastrow and Clay argued that the name is West Semitic. Thompson's preface calls him an 'Ogre'. Mesopotamian art depicts his face as a mass of coiled entrails, and he was a figure in divination. In the poem he is not simply evil: he is the legitimate guardian of the gods' forest, protected by seven auras of terror. The Sulaymaniyah fragment shows his forest filled with animal 'music', which George suggests makes him more like a foreign king at his court. The heroes' killing of him, despite his plea for mercy, provokes Enlil's anger and Enkidu's death.

title: Humbaba's roar, fire and breath
greek: rigimsu abubu, pisu girrum, napissu mutum
short: 'His roar is a whirlwind, fire is his mouth, his breath is death': the refrain describing Humbaba. Modern editions read 'Deluge', not 'whirlwind'.
body: The Akkadian word abubu, which Thompson renders 'whirlwind', is in fact the regular term for the Flood, the cosmic deluge of Tablet XI. George therefore translates 'his voice is the Deluge'. The refrain is repeated by Enkidu and by the elders, a typical device of oral-style narrative. It casts Humbaba as a force of nature as well as a monster. The verbal link to the Flood is suggestive: both are destructive instruments of Enlil.

title: Enlil's guardian
short: Humbaba is Enlil's appointee: attacking him is a challenge to the god who will later demand Enkidu's death.
body: The detail matters for the plot. In Tablet VII (in George's text, preserved partly from a Hittite version) Anu and Enlil decide that one of the two friends must die for killing Humbaba and the Bull of Heaven, and Enlil chooses Enkidu. Gilgamish's piety toward Shamash, who supports the expedition, thus collides with Enlil's authority. Thompson's arrangement leaves this council very fragmentary.

anchor: Liveth for aye in the daylight
title: 'Only the gods live forever'
short: Gilgamish answers Enkidu's fear with the poem's first statement on mortality: gods live forever, man's days are numbered, his deeds are wind.
body: In the Yale tablet's lines (George 2003) only the gods live forever with the Sun-god, human days are numbered, and human deeds are wind; this is the young hero's philosophy: since death is certain, one must win a lasting name. The irony is that after Enkidu's death the same knowledge will drive Gilgamish to seek bodily immortality. The phrase 'all that they do is but wind' has often been compared with Ecclesiastes ('all is vanity and vexation of spirit'), though a direct link is not proven.

title: Establishing a name
short: Gilgamish's motive is fame: 'if I fall, I shall have established my name' for his children to tell.
body: The idiom suma sakanu, 'to set up a name', referred both to fame and to memorials (inscriptions, statues). It is the Mesopotamian counterpart of Greek kleos aphthiton, 'imperishable fame'. The young Gilgamish here imagines his children asking him to tell the tale; the passage is often compared to Sarpedon's speech in the Iliad (12.322-328), where certain death makes heroic action meaningful. By the end of the poem the 'name' has been achieved not by the killing of Humbaba alone, but by the written record of the whole quest.

title: The giant weapons
short: The craftsmen cast axes of three talents and swords of two: impossible weights that show the heroes' superhuman strength.
body: A talent (biltu) weighed about 30 kg and a mina (manu) about half a kilo, one sixtieth of a talent. Axes of three talents (about 90 kg) and blades of thirty minas are deliberate hyperbole; each hero is 'laden with ten talents', some 300 kg. Thompson translates the Akkadian units directly. The Old Babylonian poem delights in such numbers, and the scene of the smiths at work also displays the city's crafts, which the heroes will need again when they bring back the cedar.

title: The Elders of Erech
short: Gilgamish consults the city's elders, who warn him against the expedition: kingship in the epic operates with an assembly.
body: The elders and the 'young men' form the city's two assemblies. Thorkild Jacobsen used such scenes (with the Sumerian poem 'Gilgamesh and Akka') to argue for a 'primitive democracy' in early Mesopotamia, in which the king had to seek consent. Here the elders speak with prudence ('thou art young'), and later they give the friends practical counsel, including the proverb that the one who goes in front saves his companion. Gilgamish answers them by laughing in the Old Babylonian text and in Thompson by 'pondering'.

title: 'Spread thine aegis': Thompson's classical diction
short: Thompson renders Gilgamish's plea for Shamash's protection with the Greek 'aegis', Zeus' protecting shield: a translator's choice, not a Babylonian image.
body: In Greek myth the aegis was the goatskin shield of Zeus and Athena; 'under the aegis of' became an English idiom for protection. Thompson often uses Greek or archaic words (hetaera, nymph, Hades, vaward, se'nnight) to give his hexameters a Homeric colour. Students should not read these as Babylonian concepts. The prayer itself, with raised hands before the Sun-god, is authentic Babylonian practice; Shamash's answer (an oracle) is lost.

title: Lugal-banda
short: Lugal-banda, an early king of Uruk later deified, is Gilgamish's father and personal god.
body: Thompson's note: 'Lugal-banda appears to be the tutelary god of Gilgamish, and possibly his father.' Modern scholarship confirms the second point: Lugal-banda, husband of Nin-sun, is named as Gilgamish's father in Sumerian tradition, and he was the hero of two Sumerian epic poems about a journey to Aratta. The elders' advice to pour water for Shamash and 'remember' Lugal-banda reflects the family religion of the time, in which a personal god protected an individual. Gilgamish later dedicates the horns of the Bull of Heaven to him (VI).

title: Digging a well and the libation of water
short: The elders tell Gilgamish to dig a well at each stop and pour cool water for Shamash: a ritual of the road.
body: Pure water from a freshly dug well was an offering appropriate to the gods. Pouring a libation to the Sun-god and remembering the personal god (Lugal-banda) keeps divine support on the journey. The ritual returns in Tablet IV-V, where at each halt the heroes dig a well and Gilgamish climbs a mountain to ask for a dream. Thompson's notes mark these lines as 'doubtful' and give literal alternatives.

title: 'He who goes in front saves his comrade'
short: The elders quote a proverb: the one who walks ahead protects his companion, so Enkidu, who knows the road, should lead.
body: 'Vaward' is archaic English for the vanguard. The saying, repeated several times (and by Gilgamish to Enkidu in Tablet IV), has the form of a proverb, and George notes such proverbial lines in the epic. It sets up the partnership: Gilgamish has the ambition, Enkidu has the knowledge of the wild. It also prepares for a painful irony, since Enkidu, who goes in front, is the one who dies.

title: The 'Palace of Splendour' (Egalmah)
short: The 'Palace of Splendour' is Nin-sun's temple, called Egalmah ('Great Palace') in Akkadian texts.
body: A temple was literally the 'house' or 'palace' of its god. The friends go hand in hand to Nin-sun, 'wise in all things', for advice and intercession. In George's text this scene also includes her adoption of Enkidu as her son, a passage unknown or unplaced in Thompson's day. The visit stresses the family structure of the epic: the divine mother intercedes with Shamash, the god who can protect her son.

title: Nin-sun's rooftop prayer
short: Nin-sun bathes, dresses in festal garments, climbs to the roof and offers incense to Shamash: a vivid description of a Babylonian prayer ritual.
body: Rooftops were places for night and sun rituals, close to the sky. Nin-sun's prayer reproaches the god for having given her son a 'restless heart', a key phrase for Gilgamish's character. She asks Shamash to protect him until he has killed Humbaba and 'destroyed the evil' the god hates, which presents the expedition as Shamash's cause. She also asks that Aa, Shamash's bride, remind him of her son. Thompson switches to shorter, blank-verse lines for this prayer, although the Akkadian original does not change its form here.

title: Aa (Aya), bride of Shamash
short: Aa (Aya) is the wife of the Sun-god; Nin-sun asks her, as 'bride', to speak to her husband on Gilgamish's behalf.
body: Thompson's note: 'The wife of the Sun-god.' Aya was the goddess of the dawn and regularly called kallatu, 'the bride'. Mesopotamian prayers often asked a god's spouse to intercede, as a petitioner at court might approach the queen. The mention reflects the divine household of Shamash at Sippar and Larsa. Her presence also reminds the reader that the Sun-god, like a human king, has a household that can be petitioned. Shamash will answer the prayer by sending the winds against Humbaba in Tablet V.
